units.title: All About Me and My Family

words.childMeaning: To shout happily to show you are pleased or to support someone.
practiceSentences: The whole class began to cheer for Sami.
Did you hear the crowd cheer at the match?
A loud cheer went up when Amal scored.
We cheer our team from the side of the field.
Nora gave a cheer when the rain finally stopped.

words.childMeaning: A round part that turns to make a cart or a vehicle move.
practiceSentences: The front wheel of my bicycle needs more air.
Which wheel is making that squeaking noise?
Leo watched the water wheel turn in the stream.
A cart with one broken wheel cannot roll straight.
Dad showed me how to change a wheel on the car.

words.childMeaning: Rising or falling very sharply, so it is hard to climb.
practiceSentences: The path to the top was steep and rocky.
Is that hill too steep for your bicycle?
Amal stopped halfway up the steep slope to rest.
A steep roof lets the heavy rain run off quickly.
We climbed the steep steps to the old lighthouse.

words.childMeaning: A dream is a picture or story that happens in your mind while you sleep.
practiceSentences: Amal had a happy dream last night.
What was your dream about?
Nora's dream felt very real.
I could not remember my dream this morning.
Sami wrote his strange dream in a notebook.

words.childMeaning: To stretch your arm out to get to something.
practiceSentences: Amal can reach the shelf if she stands on her toes.
Can you reach the ball under the bench?
“Reach up, then reach down to your feet,” said Teacher Yasmin.
I reach for my water bottle after every race.
Tall sunflowers reach towards the warm sunshine.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling a little cross about something that keeps bothering you.
practiceSentences: Sami felt annoyed when his pencil broke again.
Why do you look so annoyed this morning?
The buzzing fly annoyed everyone in the room.
Mum was annoyed that the taps were left running.
I get annoyed when my brother hides my shoes.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling very worried, with lots of worried thoughts that will not go away.
practiceSentences: Waiting for the exam results made me feel very anxious.
Nora felt anxious as the storm clouds gathered overhead.
Why were you anxious about the spelling test?
"When I feel anxious, I take deep breaths," said Maya.
I was anxious about the results until Father hugged me.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Happy and bright in the way you look, speak and act.
practiceSentences: Nora gave us a cheerful wave from the gate.
What a cheerful song that is!
The cheerful yellow walls made the room feel warm.
Teacher Yasmin has a cheerful voice in the morning.
Even in the rain, Leo stayed cheerful all day.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling very happy and pleased about something.
practiceSentences: Amal was delighted with her new library card.
Were you delighted by the surprise, Mina?
Grandma looked delighted when we sang for her.
We were delighted that the trip was not cancelled.
A delighted smile spread across Sami's face.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Sure you will finish something, and not ready to give up.
practiceSentences: Nora was determined to finish the race.
Are you determined to learn the whole poem?
A determined runner keeps going when her legs ache.
Leo was determined to fix the broken gate himself.
Amal stayed determined even after two mistakes.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Eager means wanting very much to do something.
practiceSentences: Leo felt eager to explore the trail.
Was Sami eager to see the mountain?
How eager they were to start the hike!
The eager children ran to the beach.
Amal was eager to open the parcel from Grandma.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling scared or afraid of something.
practiceSentences: The loud thunder frightened the little puppy.
Were you frightened by the dark corridor?
Sami felt frightened before his first speech.
A frightened bird flew straight into the window.
Nothing frightened Amal more than the deep water.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling thankful for something kind that someone has done.
practiceSentences: We are grateful for our teachers.
Are you grateful for your friends?
How grateful he looked after the help!
Sami felt grateful for the cold juice.
Omar looked surprised and grateful.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling sorry and uneasy because you know you did something wrong.
practiceSentences: Leo felt guilty about forgetting his friend's birthday.
Do you feel guilty when you break a promise?
A guilty look crossed Sami's face at once.
Amal felt guilty for eating the last mango.
Saying sorry helped Nora feel less guilty.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling upset because someone else has something you want.
practiceSentences: Sami felt jealous of his sister's new bicycle.
Are you jealous that Nora won the prize?
A jealous feeling is hard, but it soon passes.
Leo tried not to feel jealous of the winning team.
Amal was jealous until she remembered her own gift.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling very sad and unhappy for a while.
practiceSentences: Losing his football boot made Leo miserable.
Why did Amal look so miserable this morning?
Cold rain and a long walk made a miserable day.
Nobody likes to feel miserable for very long.
A warm drink helped the miserable puppy settle.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Calm, quiet and free from fighting or trouble.
practiceSentences: The garden is peaceful early in the morning.
Was the lake peaceful when you arrived?
A peaceful classroom helps everyone think clearly.
Grandma likes the peaceful hour after sunset.
They settled their argument in a peaceful way.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: If you feel pleased, you feel happy and glad about something that happened.
practiceSentences: Sami felt pleased after sharing his idea.
Was Teacher Yasmin pleased with the class?
Amal's mother was very pleased with her.
What a pleased smile that is!
Nora looked pleased with her finished painting.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Calm and comfortable, with nothing making you worried.
practiceSentences: Amal felt relaxed after the long swim.
Do you feel relaxed on a Friday afternoon?
The relaxed cat slept in the warm sunshine.
Leo looked relaxed once the test was over.
Slow breathing helps me feel relaxed again.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Feeling a little nervous around people you do not know.
practiceSentences: Mina was shy on her first day at school.
Are you shy when you meet new people?
The shy boy stood quietly beside the door.
Amal felt shy about reading aloud to the class.
Even a shy pupil can speak up in a small group.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Not sensible, a little foolish or funny.
practiceSentences: That is a silly joke, Daniel!
Did Maya make a silly mistake in her spelling?
We laughed at the silly camel in the story.
Nobody wants to make a silly mistake in the contest.
A silly hat made everybody laugh.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Brave enough to do something even when you feel afraid.
practiceSentences: It was courageous of Nora to admit her mistake.
Who was the most courageous person in the story?
A courageous firefighter carried the child outside.
Sami made a courageous choice to speak the truth.
You are courageous when you try again after failing.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Happy to share what you have, or to give things to others.
practiceSentences: It was generous of Nora to lend me her coat.
The generous baker gave extra bread to the poor family.
Who was generous enough to share their umbrella today?
"A generous heart is never empty," said the teacher.
My generous friend gave me half of her sandwich.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Always standing by someone you care about, even when it is hard.
practiceSentences: A loyal friend stays with you on a bad day.
Is your dog loyal to everyone or just to you?
Nora is loyal to her team, win or lose.
The loyal helper never let the shopkeeper down.
Sami stayed loyal to Leo after the argument.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Trusted to look after something and to do it properly.
practiceSentences: Amal is responsible for feeding the class fish.
Who is responsible for locking the gate?
A responsible pupil returns library books on time.
Leo felt responsible for his younger brother.
Being responsible means people can depend on you.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Only caring about yourself and not about how other people feel.
practiceSentences: Keeping the whole box of crayons would be selfish.
The selfish king in the story kept all the water.
Is it selfish to want the swing all break time?
"Sharing stops us from being selfish," said Mother.
I felt selfish after hiding the coloured pencils, so I apologised.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Showing good sense and thinking carefully before you act.
practiceSentences: Leo made a sensible suggestion about the vote.
Was that a sensible choice, Amal?
What a sensible idea, Sami!
It is sensible to wear a coat in the rain.
A sensible plan saves time later.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Kind, because you stop and think about what other people need.
practiceSentences: It was thoughtful of Amal to help Sami try again.
The thoughtful boy saved a seat for his friend.
Was it thoughtful of Maya to share her umbrella?
Mum said, "A thoughtful guest brings a small gift."
I was thoughtful and carried Grandma's shopping home.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Not nice or gentle, and likely to hurt someone's feelings.
practiceSentences: Leo's brother never says an unkind word.
Was that comment unkind or just honest?
How unkind that joke was!
Nobody wants to be unkind to a new pupil.
An unkind word can hurt for a long time.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Not fair, so that somebody is treated worse than the others.
practiceSentences: It felt unfair that only one team got a prize.
Was the referee's decision unfair, Daniel?
An unfair rule makes everybody unhappy.
Nora thought the extra homework was unfair.
We changed the game because the sides were unfair.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: The warm feeling between people who are friends.
practiceSentences: Their friendship began on the very first day.
What makes a friendship last a long time?
A true friendship survives a small argument.
Amal values her friendship with Nora most of all.
Sharing and listening help a friendship grow.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: The way a person acts towards other people.
practiceSentences: Kind behaviour helps everyone feel safe at school.
Good behaviour means sharing, listening, and speaking kindly.
Was your behaviour kind during playtime today?
The teacher said, "Your behaviour made me very proud."
My behaviour improves when I remember to be patient.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: Something that happens because of what somebody did before.
practiceSentences: A consequence of the rain was a flooded path.
What was the consequence of leaving the gate open?
Every choice has a consequence, said Teacher Yasmin.
The consequence of hard work was a better mark.
Leo faced the consequence of forgetting his kit.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: A moment when people do not think the same thing.
practiceSentences: A small disagreement began over the last chair.
How did you settle the disagreement, Sami?
Their disagreement ended with a friendly handshake.
The class had a disagreement about the new rule.
A disagreement is not the same as a quarrel.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: The act of being kind and helpful to somebody.
practiceSentences: One small act of kindness can start many more.
What kindness did you notice in the playground today?
“Kindness is free, so give extra when you can,” said Nora.
My jar of kindness notes is almost full now.
Teacher Yasmin thanked the class for their kindness to Amal.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: The way two people know and treat each other.
practiceSentences: Amal has a close relationship with her grandmother.
How would you describe your relationship with Leo?
A good relationship is built on trust.
Their relationship grew stronger after the trip.
Sami has a warm relationship with his young cousin.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: People working together and helping each other reach a goal.
practiceSentences: Good teamwork made the project easier, didn't it?
Teacher Yasmin talked to us about teamwork.
Our class learned that teamwork matters more than winning.
Good teamwork made our group feel proud.
Teamwork turned a hard job into an easy one.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: A person in your family, such as an aunt, a cousin or a grandparent.
practiceSentences: My favourite relative is my aunt in Mombasa.
Is that relative coming to the wedding?
Every relative brought a dish to the party.
Nora stayed with a relative during the holiday.
A cousin is the relative closest to my own age.

words.group: Words: how we feel and how we treat people
words.childMeaning: A person you have never met before.
practiceSentences: Never walk away with a stranger, said Mum.
Was the visitor a stranger or a friend?
A kind stranger helped Amal find the station.
The stranger at the gate turned out to be Uncle.
Sami felt shy talking to a stranger.

words.childMeaning: A word you use to talk about doing something to or for you.
practiceSentences: I tied my shoes myself.
Should I do this myself?
Nora said, "I made this myself!"
I taught myself to ride a bike.
I will read a whole chapter book by myself.

words.childMeaning: The word used to talk about the very person you are speaking to.
practiceSentences: Did you make this cake yourself?
Take care of yourself on the trip.
Look at yourself in the mirror, Sami!
You should be proud of yourself, Nora.
Can you tell us a little about yourself?

words.childMeaning: Used to say a boy or a man did something on his own.
practiceSentences: Leo built the whole model himself.
Did Sami write the story himself?
Dad repaired the broken gate himself.
Daniel poured the juice himself.
The little boy dressed himself for school.

words.childMeaning: Used to say that a girl or woman did something without help from anyone else.
practiceSentences: Nora tied her shoes herself this morning.
Did Mina finish the drawing herself?
My mother cooked dinner herself tonight.
Amal was proud she had done it herself.
Mina wrote the invitation herself.

words.childMeaning: The very same thing that was already mentioned.
practiceSentences: The tool itself was easy to use.
Did the beach itself feel warm under their feet?
What a huge measurement, the beach itself was so long!
Sami said the answer itself was the real clue.
The door swung open by itself in the wind.

words.childMeaning: Used to say that we did something on our own.
practiceSentences: We painted the classroom ourselves.
Shall we walk to the market ourselves?
We made the decorations ourselves this year.
Amal said we could carry the boxes ourselves.
We taught ourselves a new song at break time.

words.group: Spelling: oa says the long o
words.childMeaning: To stay on top of water without sinking.
practiceSentences: My paper boat can float.
Will this stone float?
Sami, watch my boat float!
I watch a leaf float away.
Ducks float easily on the pond.

words.group: Spelling: oa says the long o
words.childMeaning: The part inside your neck that food and air pass through.
practiceSentences: A hot drink helped Amal's sore throat.
Does your throat hurt when you swallow?
Sami cleared his throat before he began to read.
The doctor asked Leo to open wide and show his throat.
Cold air can make your throat feel dry.

words.group: Spelling: oa says the long o
words.childMeaning: A person who trains a team and helps them play better.
practiceSentences: Our coach showed us how to pass the ball.
Is the coach coming to the match on Friday?
The coach praised Nora for trying so hard.
A good coach helps every player improve.
Sami thanked the coach after the game.

words.group: Spelling: oa says the long o
words.childMeaning: Bread that has been cooked until it is brown and crisp.
practiceSentences: Amal had toast and honey for breakfast.
Would you like your toast with butter?
The smell of warm toast filled the kitchen.
Leo burnt the toast and had to start again.
Two slices of toast are enough for me.

words.childMeaning: A book that lists words and explains what they mean.
practiceSentences: Look up the new word in your dictionary.
Which dictionary does our class use?
Amal found the word curious in the dictionary.
A dictionary puts every word in alphabet order.
Teacher Yasmin keeps a big dictionary on her desk.

words.childMeaning: A small book of blank pages for writing things down.
practiceSentences: Sami writes the date at the top of his notebook.
Have you filled your whole notebook already?
Nora keeps a notebook for her best ideas.
My notebook has a red cover and thin lines.
Write the answer neatly in your notebook.

words.childMeaning: A book with exercises in it for you to complete.
practiceSentences: Open your workbook at page twelve, please.
Did you finish the workbook page last night?
Amal's workbook was full of neat handwriting.
We do one workbook exercise every morning.
Leo left his workbook on the classroom shelf.

words.childMeaning: A book you use in class to learn about a subject.
practiceSentences: Our science textbook explains how volcanoes work.
Which page of the textbook shows the diagram?
Sami covered his new textbook with brown paper.
Leave your textbook open at chapter nine.
The maths textbook has answers at the back.

words.childMeaning: One part of a long book, with its own number or title.
practiceSentences: Amal read the first chapter before bedtime.
Which chapter did you enjoy the most?
Each chapter of the book begins with a picture.
Leo finished chapter four in one evening.
The last chapter explained the whole mystery.

words.childMeaning: The list at the front of a book that shows what is inside.
practiceSentences: Check the contents page to find the chapter.
Where is the contents list in this book?
The contents page gave every heading a number.
Amal used the contents to find the poem quickly.
A good contents page saves you a lot of time.

words.childMeaning: The list at the back of a book that shows where to find things.
practiceSentences: Look in the index to find the word planet.
Does this book have an index at the back?
The index lists every page about deserts.
Sami used the index instead of reading it all.
An index is always in alphabet order.

words.childMeaning: The title written at the top of a page or a piece of writing.
practiceSentences: Write a clear heading at the top of your page.
What heading did you choose for your report?
Each heading is written in bigger letters.
Amal underlined the heading with a red pen.
A good heading tells you what the part is about.

words.childMeaning: A label is a short piece of writing that names or explains a picture or object.
practiceSentences: Every picture needs one clear label.
Where is the label for this chart, Sami?
What a tidy label, Leo!
I added a label to each page of my folder.
Add one picture and one clear label to each page.

words.childMeaning: A simple drawing that explains how something works.
practiceSentences: The diagram showed each part of the plant.
Can you label every part of this diagram?
Sami copied the diagram into his notebook.
A clear diagram is easier than a long explanation.
Our textbook has a diagram of the human ear.

words.childMeaning: A chart is a picture or table that shows information clearly.
practiceSentences: Sami checked the chart before he answered.
Whose chart is on the classroom wall?
Look at that chart, Leo!
The chart showed rain in March.
A chart on the wall shows our reading progress.

words.childMeaning: A drawing that uses bars or lines to compare numbers.
practiceSentences: The graph shows how much rain fell each month.
Which month is highest on the graph?
Nora drew a graph of our favourite fruits.
A graph makes the numbers easy to compare.
Read the graph carefully before you answer.

words.childMeaning: A photograph is a picture taken with a camera.
practiceSentences: She has seen a photograph of snow on a mountain.
Do you have a photograph of the trip?
What a lovely photograph this is!
Sami printed the photograph for her book.
Amal framed the photograph of her grandmother.

words.childMeaning: A machine that takes photographs or films moving pictures.
practiceSentences: Leo pointed the camera at the tall tree.
Whose camera is this on the desk?
The camera caught Amal in the middle of a laugh.
A camera needs good light to work well.
Sami borrowed a camera for the school trip.

words.childMeaning: A machine that plays sound sent through the air.
practiceSentences: Grandma listens to the radio every morning.
Can you turn the radio down a little?
The radio said heavy rain was coming.
We heard our teacher speak on the radio.
A radio needs no pictures, only sound.

words.childMeaning: A machine that shows moving pictures with sound.
practiceSentences: The football match is on television tonight.
How long do you watch television each day?
Amal saw a programme about whales on television.
Turn the television off before you go out.
Our television sits in the corner of the room.

words.childMeaning: A huge network that joins computers all over the world.
practiceSentences: We used the internet to find facts about Kenya.
Is the internet working in the library today?
The internet lets Amal write to her cousin.
Ask a grown-up before you use the internet.
Sami found the answer on the internet in seconds.

words.childMeaning: A place on the internet where you can read or watch things.
practiceSentences: Our school website shows the term dates.
Which website did you use for your project?
The website has a photograph of every class.
Nora built a website about her favourite birds.
A safe website is one your teacher has checked.

words.childMeaning: A message you send to somebody through a computer.
practiceSentences: Amal sent an email to her aunt in Nairobi.
Did you read the email from Teacher Yasmin?
An email arrives in seconds, not days.
Leo wrote a polite email to the museum.
Check your email for the trip letter.

words.childMeaning: A set of papers or computer work kept together.
practiceSentences: Save the file before you close the computer.
Where did you put the file about our project?
Sami opened the file and found his story.
Each file has a name so you can find it.
Amal keeps a file of her best writing.

words.childMeaning: A folder is a cover that holds your papers together.
practiceSentences: Teacher Yasmin gave every child a green folder.
Where is your reading folder, Amal?
Nora's folder was full of neat drawings!
I keep my best work in a blue folder.
Put the loose pages back in your folder.

words.childMeaning: A piece of writing that holds important information.
practiceSentences: Dad signed the document at the office.
Is this document the one we need today?
The document listed every child in the class.
Amal typed a short document about her hobby.
Keep the document safe inside the folder.

words.childMeaning: A machine that puts writing or pictures onto paper.
practiceSentences: The printer made a loud noise and stopped.
Is there any paper left in the printer?
Sami sent his story to the printer.
Our printer can print in black or colour.
Wait by the printer for your photograph.

words.childMeaning: A flat screen you touch to read, watch and play.
practiceSentences: The words on the tablet are big and clear.
May I read my story on the tablet?
“Put the tablet down at bedtime,” said Amal's mother.
I play a spelling game on my tablet with my father.
Our class shares one tablet for the word hunt.

words.childMeaning: Something built from parts that work together to do a job.
practiceSentences: A washing machine cleans clothes with water.
Which machine makes that humming sound?
The machine folded the paper very neatly.
Leo drew a machine with wheels and levers.
Every machine needs power to work.

words.childMeaning: A thing you use to help you do a job.
practiceSentences: Which tool should Sami use to measure the desk?
Maths is a tool we use every single day.
What a useful tool that metre stick is!
Nora picked the right tool for the challenge.
A hammer is a tool for knocking in nails.

words.childMeaning: The tools and things you need to do a job.
practiceSentences: The science equipment is kept in the cupboard.
Did you collect the equipment for the test?
Sports equipment must be put away neatly.
A doctor carries special equipment in her bag.
We share the equipment between two tables.

words.childMeaning: A piece of work you plan and finish over some time.
practiceSentences: Our class project is about African animals.
When is your project due, Nora?
Amal spent two weeks on her science project.
A good project needs a plan before you start.
Sami showed his project to the whole school.

words.childMeaning: Something you do, for fun or for learning.
practiceSentences: My favourite activity is painting.
Which activity will you choose today?
The first activity was a spelling game.
Every activity in the book has a picture.
Swimming is a healthy activity for children.

words.childMeaning: A job you are asked to finish.
practiceSentences: Teacher Yasmin gave the class a writing task.
Have you finished your task yet, Leo?
The task took only ten minutes to complete.
Each task is written on the board.
Amal likes a task she can do on her own.

words.childMeaning: One thing that shows what the others are like.
practiceSentences: Give me one example of a wild animal.
Can you think of an example, Sami?
The teacher wrote an example on the board.
This poem is a good example of a rhyme.
Amal used an example to explain her idea.

words.childMeaning: A sentence that tells you what to do.
practiceSentences: Read every instruction before you begin.
Which instruction did you find hardest?
The first instruction says to open your book.
Nora followed each instruction very carefully.
One clear instruction is better than three.

words.childMeaning: What happens in the end, because of what came before.
practiceSentences: The result of the match was a draw.
What was the result of your experiment?
Amal waited nervously for the result.
Hard work gave Sami a better result.
We wrote the result at the bottom of the chart.

words.childMeaning: Something you get wrong by accident.
practiceSentences: Everybody makes a mistake now and then.
Was that a mistake or a good guess?
Leo spotted one spelling mistake on the poster.
A mistake helps you learn if you fix it.
Amal made no mistake in her whole test.

words.childMeaning: A change you make to put a mistake right.
practiceSentences: Write your correction neatly underneath.
Did you make the correction in red pen?
One small correction fixed the whole sentence.
Teacher Yasmin marked a correction on my page.
A correction shows that you have learned.

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: Used to say that you and the others did something on your own.
practiceSentences: You made these cards yourselves!
Did you build the model yourselves?
Help yourselves to the fruit, children.
You should all be proud of yourselves.
Look at yourselves in the big mirror.

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: Used to say that people did something on their own.
practiceSentences: The children tidied the room themselves.
Did they write the play themselves?
Nora and Leo made the poster themselves.
They taught themselves a new song.
Ducks clean themselves in the pond.

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: A person who is not named or known.
practiceSentences: Amal is kind when someone is tired or busy.
Have you ever helped someone in trouble?
Sami, is someone knocking at the door?
Someone left flowers on the teacher's desk.
Someone must lock the classroom door.

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: Any person at all, no matter who.
practiceSentences: Mum asks if anyone needs help at home.
Does anyone know the answer?
Nora, has anyone seen my pencil?
Nobody wanted to disturb anyone during the quiet time.
Can anyone here speak Swahili?

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: Every single person in a group.
practiceSentences: Everyone in our class enjoys the library.
Is everyone ready to start?
Everyone clapped when Amal finished reading.
The teacher thanked everyone for helping.
Everyone brought a small gift for Mina.

words.group: Words that stand for people and things
words.childMeaning: Not one single person.
practiceSentences: Nobody was waiting at the gate.
Why did nobody answer the question?
Nobody knew the answer except Leo.
Nobody minded the rain during the walk.
Nobody in Grade 3 had seen the sea before.

words.childMeaning: The surface of the earth that you walk on.
practiceSentences: Amal picked the books up off the ground.
Is the ground wet after the rain?
Nora sat on the ground to tie her shoe.
Leaves covered the ground near the school gate.
The books and pencils spilled across the ground.

words.childMeaning: Shaped like a circle or a ball.
practiceSentences: The round stone rolled down the path.
Is that ball perfectly round?
Look at that big round pumpkin!
We drew a round face on the paper.
Nora cut the paper into a round shape.

words.childMeaning: To hit something hard, again and again.
practiceSentences: Waves pound the rocks during a storm.
Did you hear the rain pound on the roof?
Leo began to pound the drum with both hands.
The workers pound the metal until it is flat.

practiceSentences: Amal remembered every detail of the story.
Which detail surprised you most?
Add one more detail to your drawing.
The map shows each street in detail.
Sami missed an important detail.

words.childMeaning: The job that something is made for, or why a person does it.
practiceSentences: The purpose of the bright box is to hold our ideas.
The purpose of a lighthouse is guiding ships safely.
What is the purpose of a spider's web?
Sami said, "The purpose of practice is getting better."
My notebook's purpose is holding all my story ideas.

words.childMeaning: The subject or idea we talk or write about.
practiceSentences: Choosing a clear topic makes the writing much easier to plan.
Our writing topic today is helping our neighbours.
Which topic did you choose for your report?
Adam said, "My topic is life by the sea."
I picked rain as my topic for the poster.

words.childMeaning: The last part, where you say what you decided.
practiceSentences: Write a short conclusion to your report.
What was the conclusion of the story?
Amal read her conclusion to the class.
The conclusion should repeat the main idea.
We reached the conclusion together.

words.childMeaning: The first part, where you say what it is about.
practiceSentences: Every report needs a clear introduction.
Did you write the introduction first?
Amal's introduction was only two lines.
The introduction tells you what to expect.
Sami rewrote his introduction twice.

words.childMeaning: A short account of the main points.
practiceSentences: Write a summary of the chapter.
Can you give a summary in three lines?
Amal's summary left out the ending.
A summary is shorter than the whole story.
Sami read his summary to the class.

words.childMeaning: A piece of writing that says what you thought of something.
practiceSentences: Amal wrote a review of her favourite book.
Did you read the review in the magazine?
A good review says why you liked it.
Sami's review of the film was very short.
We write a review after every class reader.

words.childMeaning: Almost the same as something else, but not exactly.
practiceSentences: These two shells look similar, but one is larger.
Is your handwriting similar to your brother's handwriting?
“Our lunchboxes are similar,” said Mina with a laugh.
I think Amal and Nora are similar in many ways.
The two roads near my home are not similar at all.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: Some person, when you do not say exactly who.
practiceSentences: Somebody left a bag by the gate.
Did somebody call my name?
Amal asked somebody for directions.
Somebody must lock the classroom door.
There is always somebody willing to help.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: Any person at all, no matter who.
practiceSentences: Can anybody answer this question?
Did anybody see my missing pencil?
Amal will help anybody who asks.
Anybody may join the reading club.
This game is easy for anybody to learn.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: Every single person.
practiceSentences: Everybody clapped at the end.
Is everybody ready to leave?
Amal thanked everybody for coming.
Everybody in the class wrote a poem.
Sami is kind to everybody he meets.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: A thing you do not name exactly.
practiceSentences: Amal found something under her desk.
Would you like something to drink?
Something strange happened at the gate.
Sami whispered something to Nora.
There is something wrong with this sum.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: Any thing at all, no matter what.
practiceSentences: Is there anything left in the box?
Amal did not say anything at all.
You may choose anything from the shelf.
Did anything happen while I was away?
Sami will eat anything except onions.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: All the things there are.
practiceSentences: Amal packed everything into her bag.
Did you remember everything for the trip?
Everything in the room was tidy.
Sami checked everything on the list.
Everything grew well after the rain.

words.group: Words that stand for something unknown
words.childMeaning: Nothing means not anything at all.
practiceSentences: Is there nothing left to eat, Sami?
Amal said, "Nothing can stop me finishing my plan."
There was nothing on the table but a lamp.
Nothing felt more calming than the quiet evening.
Nothing grew in the dry, cracked soil.

words.childMeaning: To hit water and make it fly up in small drops.
practiceSentences: Leo likes to splash in the puddles after rain.
Did the crab splash into the water when you got close?
Cool water can splash onto your feet at the beach.
Careful, that wave might splash you!
Amal made a huge splash in the pool.

words.childMeaning: A thin cord used for tying things.
practiceSentences: Amal tied the parcel with string.
Do you have a piece of string?
The kite needs a longer string.
Sami cut the string with scissors.
A ball of string sat on the shelf.

words.childMeaning: A very thin line of cotton used for sewing.
practiceSentences: Mum threaded the needle with blue thread.
Which thread matches this cloth?
Amal sewed the button with strong thread.
A loose thread hung from his sleeve.
The thread snapped halfway through.

words.childMeaning: A huge sea animal that blows water high in the air.
practiceSentences: A blue whale is the largest animal on Earth.
How long can a whale hold its breath?
Amal read about a whale that sang.
The whale dived beneath the cold waves.
Sami drew a whale beside a small boat.

words.childMeaning: All of something, with no part left out.
practiceSentences: Amal read the whole book in one day.
Did you eat the whole mango?
The whole class cheered loudly.
It rained for a whole week.
Sami spent the whole morning drawing.

words.childMeaning: A word that describes a noun.
practiceSentences: Bright is an adjective in that sentence.
Which adjective describes the weather?
Amal used one adjective for each animal.
An adjective tells you more about a thing.
Choose a better adjective than nice.

words.childMeaning: A word that tells you how something is done.
practiceSentences: Slowly is an adverb in that sentence.
Which adverb shows how she walked?
Amal added an adverb to her sentence.
An adverb often ends with the letters ly.
Use an adverb to describe the running.

words.childMeaning: All the letters we use, from A to Z.
practiceSentences: The alphabet has twenty-six letters.
Can you say the alphabet backwards?
Amal sang the alphabet with the class.
A dictionary follows the alphabet.
Sami wrote the whole alphabet neatly.

words.childMeaning: A small word such as a, an or the, used before a noun.
practiceSentences: The word the is an article.
Which article goes before apple?
Amal circled every article in the sentence.
An article comes before a naming word.
We use the article an before a vowel sound.

words.childMeaning: A short line of writing that explains a picture.
practiceSentences: The caption named everyone in the photograph.
What caption would you write for this picture?
Amal added a caption under her drawing.
Keep the caption short and clear.
Each caption sits below its own photograph.

words.childMeaning: A small mark ( , ) used to show a pause or to separate items in a list.
practiceSentences: I wrote rice, lamb, and dates with a comma between them.
A comma tells the reader to pause for a moment.
Where should the comma go in this long sentence?
"Put a comma between the items in your list," said Teacher Yasmin.
I forgot the comma, so my sentence looked confusing.

words.childMeaning: A sentence that tells somebody to do something.
practiceSentences: Sit down is a command.
Can you write a command sentence?
Amal used a command in her instructions.
A command often begins with a verb.
Close the door is a short command.

words.childMeaning: A word such as and or but that joins parts of a sentence.
practiceSentences: And is the commonest conjunction.
Which conjunction joins these two ideas?
Amal used the conjunction because.
A conjunction holds two sentences together.
But is a useful conjunction.

words.childMeaning: A book where you write what happens each day.
practiceSentences: Amal writes in her diary every night.
Where do you keep your diary?
The diary had a small silver lock.
Sami wrote about the trip in his diary.
A diary helps you remember details.

words.childMeaning: A conversation between two or more people.
practiceSentences: The dialogue between the two friends felt real.
Can you write the dialogue for this scene?
Amal read the dialogue aloud with Nora.
Speech marks show where dialogue begins.
The dialogue in that story made me laugh.

words.childMeaning: Stories that are made up and not real.
practiceSentences: Our teacher keeps fiction and true books on separate shelves.
The library keeps fiction books on the blue shelves.
Do you prefer fiction or true stories about animals?
"Good fiction can take you anywhere," said the librarian.
I am writing a fiction story about a talking camel.

words.childMeaning: A word list at the back of a book with meanings.
practiceSentences: Check the glossary for that hard word.
Does this book have a glossary?
Amal added a glossary to her project.
The glossary explains every science word.
A glossary is arranged in alphabet order.

words.childMeaning: The rules for how we put words together to speak and write.
practiceSentences: The grammar contest tested verbs, questions, and small joining words.
Good grammar helps our sentences make sense.
Did you finish the grammar exercise on verbs?
The teacher said, "Check your grammar before handing in."
I am getting better at grammar every week.

words.childMeaning: A word that names a person, place or thing.
practiceSentences: School is a noun in that sentence.
Which noun names the animal?
Amal underlined every noun in red.
A noun can be a person, place or thing.
Sami wrote ten nouns in a list.

words.childMeaning: A short group of words used together.
practiceSentences: In the garden is a phrase, not a sentence.
Which phrase describes the place?
Amal repeated the same phrase twice.
A phrase has no verb of its own.
Sami learned a new phrase in Swahili.

words.childMeaning: The form of a word that means more than one.
practiceSentences: Books is the plural of book.
What is the plural of child?
Amal wrote each plural correctly.
Most plurals end with the letter s.
The plural of foot is feet.

words.childMeaning: Showing that something belongs to somebody.
practiceSentences: Amal's bag uses a possessive.
Which possessive shows it is hers?
A possessive often needs an apostrophe.
My and your are possessive words.
Sami wrote the possessive form neatly.

words.childMeaning: A short part added to the front of a word.
practiceSentences: Un is a prefix in unhappy.
Which prefix means not?
Amal added a prefix to change the meaning.
A prefix goes before the main word.
Re is the prefix in rewrite.

words.childMeaning: A word that stands in place of a naming word.
practiceSentences: She is a pronoun in that sentence.
Which pronoun replaces Amal?
Amal used a pronoun instead of the name.
A pronoun saves you repeating a noun.
They is a plural pronoun.

words.childMeaning: The marks we use in writing, like full stops and commas.
practiceSentences: Check the punctuation in your sentence.
Which punctuation ends a question?
Amal corrected the punctuation in red.
Good punctuation helps the reader.
A comma is one kind of punctuation.

words.childMeaning: A person who reads, or a book used for reading.
practiceSentences: Amal is a fast and careful reader.
Which reader are we using this term?
A good reader stops to think.
Sami became a stronger reader this year.
Every reader chose a different book.

words.childMeaning: The form of a word that means only one.
practiceSentences: Book is the singular of books.
What is the singular of mice?
Amal wrote the singular beside the plural.
A singular noun names just one thing.
Child is singular and children is plural.

words.childMeaning: A talk given out loud to a group of people.
practiceSentences: Amal gave a short speech to the class.
Did you enjoy the head teacher's speech?
A good speech has a clear beginning.
Sami practised his speech in the mirror.
The speech lasted only two minutes.

words.childMeaning: The correct order of letters in a word.
practiceSentences: Check the spelling before you finish.
Which spelling is right, Nora?
Amal won the spelling contest.
A dictionary shows you every spelling.
Sami practises his spelling each night.

words.childMeaning: A short part added to the end of a word.
practiceSentences: Ly is a suffix in slowly.
Which suffix means full of?
Amal added a suffix to make a new word.
A suffix comes after the main word.
The suffix ing shows it is happening now.

words.childMeaning: A word that means almost the same as another word.
practiceSentences: A synonym for happy is joyful.
Can you give a synonym for enormous?
Amal found a synonym in the dictionary.
Use a synonym instead of repeating nice.
Big and large are a synonym pair.

words.childMeaning: The form of a verb that shows when it happened.
practiceSentences: Walked is the past tense of walk.
Which tense is this sentence in?
Amal changed the tense to the past.
A tense tells you when the action happened.
Sami wrote the whole story in one tense.

words.childMeaning: A word that shows an action or a state.
practiceSentences: Run is a verb in that sentence.
Which verb tells you what she did?
Amal underlined every verb in blue.
A verb is often called an action word.
Sami listed ten verbs from the passage.

words.childMeaning: All the words a person knows and uses.
practiceSentences: Reading grows your vocabulary quickly.
How many words are in your vocabulary?
Amal keeps a vocabulary notebook.
A wide vocabulary helps your writing.
We learn new vocabulary every week.

words.childMeaning: Writing about real things that are true.
practiceSentences: This nonfiction book explains volcanoes.
Do you prefer nonfiction or stories?
Amal borrowed a nonfiction book about bees.
Nonfiction gives you facts, not made-up tales.
The nonfiction shelf is near the window.

words.childMeaning: The order in which things happen.
practiceSentences: Put the pictures in the right sequence.
What is the sequence of the story?
Amal wrote the sequence of each step.
A sequence shows what comes first and next.
Sami mixed up the sequence of events.

words.childMeaning: Things put out where people can see them.
practiceSentences: Our display shows work from every class.
Which display did you like best?
Amal arranged the display by the door.
The museum display had ancient coins.
Sami stood beside his display table.

words.childMeaning: A plan of what will happen at an event.
practiceSentences: The concert programme lists every song.
Have you seen the programme for sports day?
Amal printed the programme for the parents.
A programme tells you what comes next.
Sami kept the programme as a souvenir.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: At any time that something happens.
practiceSentences: Come and see us whenever you like.
Whenever it rains, the path floods.
Amal smiles whenever she sees a dog.
Whenever did you find the time?
Sami helps whenever he is asked.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: In or to any place at all.
practiceSentences: Sit wherever you find a space.
Wherever Amal goes, her book goes too.
You may play wherever it is safe.
Wherever did you put my pencil?
Sami follows his brother wherever he goes.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: Any person at all, when it does not matter who.
practiceSentences: Whoever finishes first may go outside.
Give the note to whoever answers the door.
Amal will thank whoever helped her.
Whoever left this bag should collect it.
Sami plays with whoever is free.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: Whatever means anything or no matter what happens.
practiceSentences: Whatever happens, we will stay together.
Choose whatever colour you like best.
Amal will eat whatever is on her plate.
Whatever will we do if it rains!
Sami reads whatever he can find.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: Less means a smaller amount of something.
practiceSentences: The path had less wind than the beach.
Is there less shade under this tree?
There is so much less rain this year!
Sami wanted less sugar in his tea.
Use less water when you wash up.

words.group: Words that mean any one at all
words.childMeaning: Least means the smallest amount or number of something.
practiceSentences: There were at least twenty children in the hall.
Did you sleep at least eight hours last night?
At least try your best, Nora!
Amal picked at least two poems for the showcase.
Sami reads for at least an hour every evening.
